To follow this tutorial, you will need a web browser.

slides.title: Prerequisites
content: Basic understanding of Artificial Intelligence concepts.
slides.narration:
Before starting, you should have a basic understanding of Artificial Intelligence.
Familiarity with Machine Learning concepts is helpful.
If not, don't worry.
We will simplify everything.
slides.image_prompt: A cartoon character with a thought bubble showing simple AI icons like a robot face or a gear.

slides.title: What is Deep Learning?
slides.narration:
So, what is Deep Learning?
It's a powerful part of AI.
It helps computers learn like humans.
Deep Learning uses special structures called Neural Networks.
These networks find very complex patterns in data.
slides.image_prompt: A cartoon brain with gears, surrounded by data bits (like 0s and 1s), a lightbulb above it, signifying intelligence.

slides.title: The Cartoon Detective Agency
slides.narration:
Let's imagine Deep Learning as a super-smart detective agency.
This agency solves tough mysteries.
Each little detective in the agency is like a 'neuron'.
They work together to find clues.
slides.image_prompt: A whimsical cartoon detective agency building, with tiny cartoon detectives peeking out windows, some with magnifying glasses.

slides.title: Meet the Neurons (Detectives)
content: A neuron is a tiny processing unit.
slides.narration:
Each neuron is a tiny, specialized cartoon character.
They receive information.
Then they process it.
Finally, they pass it on to others.
Think of them as busy little workers.
slides.image_prompt: A single, friendly cartoon character detective with a magnifying glass, wearing a trench coat and hat, looking thoughtful.

slides.title: Layers of Detectives
content: Hidden Layers: Process and find patterns.
Output Layer: Gives the final answer.
slides.narration:
These detectives are not alone.
They are organized into teams, or 'layers'.
Each layer has a special job.
They pass clues from one team to the next.
slides.image_prompt: Three distinct groups (layers) of cartoon detectives, arranged vertically, with arrows showing information flow between layers. Each layer has a slightly different look to signify its role.

slides.title: The Input Layer (The 'Eyes')
slides.narration:
The first layer is the Input Layer.
Think of them as the 'eyes' of our agency.
They receive raw data or initial clues.
They don't process much.
They just observe and pass on.
slides.image_prompt: A row of cartoon detectives with exaggerated big eyes, holding a magnifying glass to raw, unorganized data, like a blurry photograph or jumbled letters.

slides.title: Hidden Layers (The 'Thinkers')
slides.narration:
Next come the Hidden Layers.
These are the 'thinkers' of our agency.
They perform complex analysis.
They extract features and find hidden patterns.
Many hidden layers make it 'deep' learning.
slides.image_prompt: Multiple rows of cartoon detectives wearing thinking caps, some pointing at boards with equations, others discussing clues. Arrows show data moving between rows.

slides.title: The Output Layer (The 'Decision Makers')
slides.narration:
Finally, we have the Output Layer.
These are the 'decision-makers'.
They give the final answer or prediction.
This is the agency's conclusion.
They present the solved mystery.
slides.image_prompt: A single cartoon detective at a desk, stamping a 'Solved!' document, with a clear answer displayed (e.g., 'This is a Cat' or 'This is a Dog').

slides.title: How They Learn (Training)
slides.narration:
How do these detectives get so smart?
They learn through training.
We give them many examples of solved cases.
They adjust their methods.
They learn from their mistakes.
slides.image_prompt: A wise cartoon mentor detective teaching a group of younger detective characters, pointing to 'case files' (data with labels like 'cat photo' labeled 'cat').

slides.title: The Learning Process (Backpropagation)
slides.narration:
This learning involves two steps.
First, they make a guess, this is the forward pass.
Then, they check if their guess was right.
If not, they find out where they went wrong.
This error correction is called backpropagation.
They adjust their connections to improve.
slides.image_prompt: Cartoon detectives passing a 'guess' forward (green arrow), then a 'correction' signal (red 'X' or red arrow) moving backward through the layers, causing characters to adjust their thinking caps.

slides.title: Activation Functions (The 'Spark')
slides.narration:
Each detective also has a 'spark'.
This spark decides if they should pass information.
It's called an activation function.
It adds complexity to their thinking.
This helps them learn very complex patterns.
slides.image_prompt: A cartoon detective with a lightbulb above its head, showing a 'spark' or 'activation' when a certain threshold is met, indicating it's passing information.

slides.title: Deep Learning in Action
slides.narration:
Deep Learning solves many real-world problems.
It helps with image recognition.
It powers natural language processing.
Self-driving cars use it.
It even aids medical diagnosis.
It's everywhere!
slides.image_prompt: A collage of cartoon icons representing: a camera recognizing a cat, a speech bubble translating languages, a self-driving car on a road, and a doctor looking at an X-ray with an AI overlay.

slides.title: Summary
content: Deep Learning uses layered Neural Networks.
slides.narration:
In summary, Deep Learning uses layered Neural Networks.
Tiny neurons process information.
They work in Input, Hidden, and Output layers.
The network learns through training.
Backpropagation helps correct errors.
This makes AI very smart.
slides.image_prompt: A simplified cartoon diagram of a neural network showing input, hidden, and output layers, with arrows indicating data flow and learning.

slides.title: Assignment
content: Imagine a new cartoon analogy for Deep Learning.
Describe its neurons, layers, and learning process.
Share your analogy with a friend.
slides.narration:
Here is a small assignment for you.
Imagine a new cartoon analogy for Deep Learning.
Describe its neurons, layers, and learning process.
How would your cartoon characters learn and improve?
Share your creative analogy with a friend.
